item.title: Open-World RPGs Give Us Bigger Worlds, But Blood of Dawnwalker Is Giving Us Something Better
item.description:
Considering how much time the open-world RPG genre has spent selling freedom by the square mile, The Blood of Dawnwalker is remarkably refreshing. That's a strange thing to admit, given Rebel Wolves' debut is clearly smaller than most of the games it will inevitably be compared to, and it hands players a literal gameplay timer on top of that. But while both of those features sound like restrictions on paper, these "restraints" are actually the reason The Blood of Dawnwalker is my most anticipated open-world RPG of the year.

To be clear, I love open-world RPGs, but that's why the genre's slow drift toward a "bigger-is-better" design philosophy has been so grating. Of course, that alone doesn't qualify my interest in Dawnwalker 's world, one Rebel Wolves itself describes as not that big, or the in-game limit of 30 days and 30 nights to save protagonist Coen's family from Brensis, the region's vampire lord. That said, the nitty-gritty details these elements imply (and what Rebel Wolves intends to achieve overall) have already made Blood of Dawnwalker one of the boldest offerings in the genre this year; one I pray ends up being influential in the long run, too.

My Most Anticipated Game of 2026 Finally Has a Release Date

I've been champing at the bit while waiting for Blood of Dawnwalker's release date, and it's finally here. Now I have to survive the wait for release.

By Joshua Duckworth

Blood of Dawnwalker Is Rightfully Bucking A Bigger Map

For context, this genre's larger problem with map size and staleness makes plenty of sense: scale is measurable, marketable, and easy to promise, even pre-release. The catch is that, as this tried-and-true system has run its course, the content filling all that space has gotten cheaper and less surprising, leaving icons and camps to clear where memorable gameplay should be. Ubisoft's "climb the tower for things to do" template is the most recognizable version of it, but the problem extends well beyond any single publisher; this certainly isn't the first time I've stressed how clearly the modern open-world genre is missing something tangible.

Big worlds aren't inherently bad, of course—plenty of players want that experience—the trouble comes down to scale and intentionality. That's something Dawnwalker 's Game Director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz has actually described before: he's been clear about how the genre's behemoths have maps that are impossible to really know every nook and cranny of, and how players end up rushing through them instead of living in them. Budgets aside, a smaller map and a tighter focus provide an opportunity for those equipped to capitalize on it; thankfully, Rebel Wolves fit that bill, considering Dawnwalker 's Vale Sangora comes in as a deliberate step-down in map size, and an equally deliberate step forward toward player freedom.

Dawnwalker Is Pitching a Package Deal

At Gamescom, Senior Quest Designer Patryk Fijalkowski plainly stated that Blood of Dawnwalker 's world "isn't that big." A great example of that: as a result, there are no mounts of any kind in the valley of Vale Sangora. But Dawnwalker is clearly a very intentional package, and even based on previews alone, it's clear the actual content on offer speaks to an ingenious sort of practicality—one keeps a project like this inside a scope a smaller studio like Rebel Wolves could realistically follow through on.

I love open-world RPGs, but that's why the genre's slow drift toward a "bigger-is-better" design philosophy has been so grating.

What's particularly striking in this case is that Blood of Dawnwalker 's world, Vale Sangora, has essentially been designed twice. The game's protagonist, Coen, is a Dawnwalker—a human by day and a vampire by night—which means that depending on which from players choose, each play space carries several distinct sets of access points based on each form's abilities, and two versions of whoever (or whatever) might be waiting inside. As players are deciding how to spend their time, which version of the world they want to inhabit will be a critical decision.

One current example of this system in practice is a quest that sends Coen hunting for a legendary sword. Eventually, the hunt leads him to its owner, Saint Mihai, who's a Dawnwalker that's entombed alive by the villagers who once revered him. He's starved through the day and regenerated each night until his mind finally gave out, and should Coen arrive in daylight, Mihai comes at you with the full Dawnwalker toolkit; after dark, their vampire form will change the encounter drastically.

Transforming the Traditional Ubisoft Tower Trope

Though it's mostly a funny aside, it's worth mentioning that Blood of Dawnwalker hasn't fully done away with the Ubisoft tower trope—but it has meaningfully evolved it. Coen can still climb one to reveal the surrounding map, but it's something that can really only happen after sundown, because walking up walls is a vampire power. To me, that's a meaningful change, and some helpful nuance considering my issue isn't that the existing formula is wrong; just cheapened.

Dawnwalker's Clock System and Time Well Spent

The crucial second part of this package is the in-game clock, especially given how it functions as a vehicle for player choice. It sounds stressful at first: each of the 30 days and nights is a bar split into 8 segments, and only actions flagged with an hourglass icon will spend one of those segments. But exploring the valley, fighting enemies, and poking through ruins cost nothing whatsoever—and any decision that will move things forward is clearly marked as such in the UI.

This is exciting, particularly because, in essence, it seems more like a unique gameplay economy that players can build playthroughs around than any sort of limitation. Plus, players have an exit at either end, as after the prologue nothing is stopping you from walking up to Brencis' castle and trying your luck against him immediately. Should players prefer the scenic route instead, day 30 is apparently more of a story branch than a hard limit, too—Tomaszkiewicz said he hopes some players let time run out entirely to see some unique content, and Piotr Kucharski, a writer at Rebel Wolves, told CNET, "In fact, we invite it, right? We want to see those people on YouTube."

The crucial second part of this package is the in-game clock, especially given how it functions as a vehicle for player choice.

This isn't an unprecedented design decision: Tomaszkiewicz has pointed to the influence of the original two Fallout games, where a player who knew the route could ignore everything and head straight for the Enclave. What's new here is the pairing, a proven structure welded to an economy where even leveling up spends a segment of daylight. How that will influence each playthrough is what makes Dawnwalker so exciting.

Smaller Worlds, Intentionality, and What Might Save a Genre From Fatigue

Ultimately, my experience with this beloved genre is that the open-world RPG has grown a little too comfortable selling acreage as a stand-in for quality and intention, and the results have started to blur together. Dawnwalker 's bet seems to be that player freedom is better measured by how many ways your choices shape the play space over time, and that such a pursuit is better suited to a world small enough to really feel that. That is remarkably refreshing already.

February 2027's New Game Releases Look Like September 2026 All Over Again
Blood of Dawnwalker's Mass Effect-Like Save Carryovers Give Its Future Massive Potential
Blood of Dawnwalker Sounds Like a Total Nightmare for RPG Completionists
Gege Akutami Is Officially Killing Off His Main Character

Of course, there is an obvious limit to what any of us actually know ahead of Blood of Dawnwalker 's actual release. The most substantial hands-on previews covered a single slice of one map across roughly four hours; most of the rest of the coverage has been hands-off, and nobody outside Rebel Wolves has actually seen what a beeline to Brensis or what a 30-day clock expiration actually looks like. But given Rebel Wolves' pedigree and how deliberately every piece of this seems to have been assembled, these are surprises I'm looking forward to answering when I can get my hands on the game when it drops September 3.

The Blood of Dawnwalker

item.title: US Army Giving Soldiers Time Off to Play GTA 6, But There's a Catch
item.description:
A flyer from a US Army battalion reportedly claimed that it would offer soldiers a four-day pass to play Grand Theft Auto 6 on release if they commit to a specific decision beforehand. As of this writing, GTA 6 is still on track to launch worldwide on Thursday, November 19, on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles.

It's no secret that GTA 6 is one of the most-anticipated games of 2026, as pre-order figures for the game continue to climb ahead of the November 19 launch. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick claimed that pre-orders for GTA 6 Ultimate Edition outnumbered GTA 6 Standard Edition , despite the latter being cheaper. However, Zelnick did not provide an exact margin for how much GTA 6 Ultimate Edition has outsold its standard counterpart. A likely reason is due to the fact that GTA 6 Ultimate Edition has exclusive content and shops that are not in the standard version.

Grand Theft Auto 6 CEO Releases Official Statement on Christmas Discounts

During a recent interview, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick discusses the possibility of discounts on Grand Theft Auto 6 for the holidays.

By Joshua Duckworth

US Army Battalion Reportedly Offering Time Off to Play GTA 6 on One Condition

While GTA 6 will be a major revenue generator for Rockstar Games, the game's pre-launch popularity has reportedly caught the attention of the US Army. According to a flyer posted by 'US Army WTF! Moments' on Instagram, The 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion (9th BEB) of Fort Stewart, Georgia, was offering soldiers stationed there an opportunity to take four days off to play Grand Theft Auto 6 from November 20 to 23. However, soldiers must sign a reenlistment contract between August 1 and November 14 to claim this pass.

The flyer was signed off by the 9th BEB's commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Ryan Hodgson, who assumed control of the battalion on July 13, 2026. In short, LtCol Hodgson has only been at the post for over a month as of this writing. The flyer's incentive window to reenlist in the US Army and get the four-day pass also operated under the assumption that GTA 6 will launch in November. Given that doubts about GTA 6 's November 19 release date still linger on social media, it is unclear if the incentive window will be moved around should such a scenario come to pass. The US Army has not officially commented on the legitimacy of the Fort Stewart flyer, so it remains to be seen if it will be honored.

The hype surrounding GTA 6 's pending launch has also spilled over to civilian businesses. On June 11, Burger Motorsports in California stated that operations would see delays during GTA 6 's launch window. The company said that customer support, social media, and general productivity would be affected due to the fact that several staff members have already requested time off to play GTA 6 .

item.title: 5 "Bad" Single-Player FPS Games That Are Fun As Hell
item.description:
I love a "bad" game that aims for the stars but hits the sea instead. During the 2000s and early 2010s, the FPS genre was booming, so every publisher and developer jumped on the Call of Duty bandwagon, though most failed to catch a ride. For each masterpiece, we got two terrible FPS games that have been utterly forgotten by time... However, a few of these failures are pretty darn entertaining in a B-movie type of way .

As the genre's blueprint was codified by the late 2000s, most FPS games from this era control well, even if everything else falls short of expectations. Consequently, revisiting these "classics" can be fairly painless, as long as you manage to find a copy somewhere and don't mind the occasional groan-worthy moments. Time to go dumpster diving!

When I say "bad," I mean these games were eviscerated by critics and maybe even players at the time. I'm not saying these shooters are actually masterpieces, but I had fun with them.

Also, while some of these games had multiplayer, they are basically single-player-only nowadays.

Legendary Should Be A Legendary FPS Game

A Monster Movie On Steroids

I'll take any opportunities to bring up Legendary , a game that sat in my Steam library for roughly a decade before I finally had nothing better to do. In 2008, Spark Unlimited became the kings of FPS trash with Turning Point: Fall of Liberty and Legendary , both of which received near-universal negativity. Although Turning Point has its moments, Legendary is the one that I would recommend seeking out, especially if you enjoy supernatural shooters that really aim big.

8 Great FPS Games You Cannot Buy Anymore

These FPS games are fantastic, but sadly, they were delisted and evaporated from the digital store shelves.

6
By Mark Sammut

You open Pandora's Box, unleashing mythological monsters all across the world; naturally, you pick up a gun and blast your way through one set piece after another. Legendary drops the ball in quite a few basic areas, including AI and gun feel, but its unapologetic over-the-top nature more than makes up for any shortcomings. The 5-hour campaign sees you take on werewolves, skyscraper-sized golems, griffins, and even a kraken, all presented with style and energy.

I never got to try Legendary 's multiplayer, but the single-player is just relentless in the best possible way.

Judge Dredd: Dredd Vs. Death Is One For The Fans

Ever "Bad" Judge Dredd Is Judge Dredd

Despite being the perfect franchise for the genre, we have only gotten two Judge Dredd FPS games, and one of them is a light-gun shooter. That means only 2003's Judge Dredd: Dredd Vs. Death qualifies , and it basically killed the franchise's video game run since we haven't gotten a new release in the last 23 years.

Look, I'm not going to pretend that Rebellion Developments crafted an underappreciated gem, nor would I recommend this game to those who cannot tell their Judge Dredds from their RoboCops. However, if you love the source material, Judge Dredd: Dredd Vs. Death does an admirable job of bringing to life Mega-City One and the Judge system, all the while embracing the comic's campiness.

Simply existing in this universe manages to do most of the heavy lifting, and the campaign allows players to soak in the vibes during its first half. The story eventually devolves into standard hallway blasting, but even that is cool since you are the law (and have his iconic sidearm).

You Are Empty Is An Incredibly Atmospheric Forgotten Shooter

An Alternate Reality FPS Game That Walked So The Likes Of Metro Could Run

Just to be clear, I don't think any of these FPS games are "bad," but I can see why they have that reputation.

You Are Empty deserved way better, and it is one of the more fascinating shooters of the mid-2000s. Developed by two Ukrainian studios, the game takes place in an alternate 1950s Soviet Union after a global experiment kills most of the population and mutates the rest into monsters. Drenched in appropriate architecture, You Are Empty 's biggest strength is its willingness to let players soak in its eerie atmosphere, which holds up pretty well.

Gameplay-wise, You Are Empty plays like, well, a rough 2000s horror shooter. The AI isn't great, and your character moves at a glacial pace that threatens to grate after a while. You never forget that you are playing a budget title that lacks the polish of Western releases of that era, but you also get to bask in the glory of creative and unsettling enemy designs that you also wouldn't see in most big-name FPS games.

6 Best Games That Completely Rewrite History, Ranked

Alternate history works wonders when paired with video games, allowing developers to completely rewrite the past to suit their ideas.

By Eman Fatima

Darkest of Days Is Like Battlefield Mixed With Doctor Who

An FPS Game That Offers Scale And Absurdity

I'm starting to sense a pattern: Nearly all these FPS games execute million-dollar premises on a shoestring budget . Honestly, that's something I like about them, as I'd rather play something that tries too much rather than tries too little.

Darkest of Days might be the weirdest FPS game of the Xbox 360 era, and that's not a statement made lightly. A Civil War soldier becomes a time cop charged with preserving history, and he heads out to stop several historical moments from drifting off course. Initially, the campaign keeps things slightly "grounded," but that eventually flies out the window as you begin to use a plasma rifle to blast through a 19th-century infantry.

Say what you want about its many problems, but Darkest of Days manages to deliver the right sense of scale for this story. Battlefields feature dozens of soldiers at a time when that wasn't guaranteed, and the story cycles through an impressive array of diverse scenarios and eras. The gameplay doesn't quite make the most of these elements, and it takes way too long to embrace the premise's silliness, but it's hard not to appreciate the effort.

Blue Estate Is Bad Taste, Good Shooting

A Rail Shooter That Proves We Need More Rail Shooters

Full disclosure, I was hesitant to include Blue Estate , as it might be the most obnoxious game I've ever played. Let's just say that if you cannot stand toilet humor, then you will not be able to get through this rail shooter with the audio on.

The story follows a mob prince and hitman who go on rampages against a Jamaican-Korean underworld gang, and the latter's presentation shoots good taste in the head. Frankly, I don't really have anything good to say about the story or characters... but I love the arcade-style gunplay.

Rail shooters aren't everyone's cup of tea, and we don't get many of them anymore. However, Blue Estate shows that the subgenre can still captivate from a gameplay perspective, and few things are as satisfying as pulling off perfect headshot combos followed by a glorious explosion. Split into only 7 chapters, the game ends way too quickly, but it's basically 3 hours of nonstop mayhem and crisp gunplay.

item.content:encoded:
I love a "bad" game that aims for the stars but hits the sea instead. During the 2000s and early 2010s, the FPS genre was booming, so every publisher and developer jumped on the Call of Duty bandwagon, though most failed to catch a ride. For each masterpiece, we got two terrible FPS games that have been utterly forgotten by time... However, a few of these failures are pretty darn entertaining in a B-movie type of way .

As the genre's blueprint was codified by the late 2000s, most FPS games from this era control well, even if everything else falls short of expectations. Consequently, revisiting these "classics" can be fairly painless, as long as you manage to find a copy somewhere and don't mind the occasional groan-worthy moments. Time to go dumpster diving!

When I say "bad," I mean these games were eviscerated by critics and maybe even players at the time. I'm not saying these shooters are actually masterpieces, but I had fun with them.

Also, while some of these games had multiplayer, they are basically single-player-only nowadays.

Legendary Should Be A Legendary FPS Game

A Monster Movie On Steroids

I'll take any opportunities to bring up Legendary , a game that sat in my Steam library for roughly a decade before I finally had nothing better to do. In 2008, Spark Unlimited became the kings of FPS trash with Turning Point: Fall of Liberty and Legendary , both of which received near-universal negativity. Although Turning Point has its moments, Legendary is the one that I would recommend seeking out, especially if you enjoy supernatural shooters that really aim big.

8 Great FPS Games You Cannot Buy Anymore

These FPS games are fantastic, but sadly, they were delisted and evaporated from the digital store shelves.

6
By Mark Sammut

You open Pandora's Box, unleashing mythological monsters all across the world; naturally, you pick up a gun and blast your way through one set piece after another. Legendary drops the ball in quite a few basic areas, including AI and gun feel, but its unapologetic over-the-top nature more than makes up for any shortcomings. The 5-hour campaign sees you take on werewolves, skyscraper-sized golems, griffins, and even a kraken, all presented with style and energy.

I never got to try Legendary 's multiplayer, but the single-player is just relentless in the best possible way.

Judge Dredd: Dredd Vs. Death Is One For The Fans

Ever "Bad" Judge Dredd Is Judge Dredd

Despite being the perfect franchise for the genre, we have only gotten two Judge Dredd FPS games, and one of them is a light-gun shooter. That means only 2003's Judge Dredd: Dredd Vs. Death qualifies , and it basically killed the franchise's video game run since we haven't gotten a new release in the last 23 years.

Look, I'm not going to pretend that Rebellion Developments crafted an underappreciated gem, nor would I recommend this game to those who cannot tell their Judge Dredds from their RoboCops. However, if you love the source material, Judge Dredd: Dredd Vs. Death does an admirable job of bringing to life Mega-City One and the Judge system, all the while embracing the comic's campiness.

Simply existing in this universe manages to do most of the heavy lifting, and the campaign allows players to soak in the vibes during its first half. The story eventually devolves into standard hallway blasting, but even that is cool since you are the law (and have his iconic sidearm).

More Games

You Are Empty Is An Incredibly Atmospheric Forgotten Shooter

An Alternate Reality FPS Game That Walked So The Likes Of Metro Could Run

Just to be clear, I don't think any of these FPS games are "bad," but I can see why they have that reputation.

You Are Empty deserved way better, and it is one of the more fascinating shooters of the mid-2000s. Developed by two Ukrainian studios, the game takes place in an alternate 1950s Soviet Union after a global experiment kills most of the population and mutates the rest into monsters. Drenched in appropriate architecture, You Are Empty 's biggest strength is its willingness to let players soak in its eerie atmosphere, which holds up pretty well.

Gameplay-wise, You Are Empty plays like, well, a rough 2000s horror shooter. The AI isn't great, and your character moves at a glacial pace that threatens to grate after a while. You never forget that you are playing a budget title that lacks the polish of Western releases of that era, but you also get to bask in the glory of creative and unsettling enemy designs that you also wouldn't see in most big-name FPS games.

6 Best Games That Completely Rewrite History, Ranked

Alternate history works wonders when paired with video games, allowing developers to completely rewrite the past to suit their ideas.

By Eman Fatima

Darkest of Days Is Like Battlefield Mixed With Doctor Who

An FPS Game That Offers Scale And Absurdity

I'm starting to sense a pattern: Nearly all these FPS games execute million-dollar premises on a shoestring budget . Honestly, that's something I like about them, as I'd rather play something that tries too much rather than tries too little.

Darkest of Days might be the weirdest FPS game of the Xbox 360 era, and that's not a statement made lightly. A Civil War soldier becomes a time cop charged with preserving history, and he heads out to stop several historical moments from drifting off course. Initially, the campaign keeps things slightly "grounded," but that eventually flies out the window as you begin to use a plasma rifle to blast through a 19th-century infantry.

Say what you want about its many problems, but Darkest of Days manages to deliver the right sense of scale for this story. Battlefields feature dozens of soldiers at a time when that wasn't guaranteed, and the story cycles through an impressive array of diverse scenarios and eras. The gameplay doesn't quite make the most of these elements, and it takes way too long to embrace the premise's silliness, but it's hard not to appreciate the effort.

Blue Estate Is Bad Taste, Good Shooting

A Rail Shooter That Proves We Need More Rail Shooters

Full disclosure, I was hesitant to include Blue Estate , as it might be the most obnoxious game I've ever played. Let's just say that if you cannot stand toilet humor, then you will not be able to get through this rail shooter with the audio on.

The story follows a mob prince and hitman who go on rampages against a Jamaican-Korean underworld gang, and the latter's presentation shoots good taste in the head. Frankly, I don't really have anything good to say about the story or characters... but I love the arcade-style gunplay.

Rail shooters aren't everyone's cup of tea, and we don't get many of them anymore. However, Blue Estate shows that the subgenre can still captivate from a gameplay perspective, and few things are as satisfying as pulling off perfect headshot combos followed by a glorious explosion. Split into only 7 chapters, the game ends way too quickly, but it's basically 3 hours of nonstop mayhem and crisp gunplay.

item.title: New Official Fallout PS5 Release Confirmed for September 15
item.description:
Fallout is getting a new PS5 release on September 15, when Fallout 76 launches its next-gen update alongside the release of Season 26, titled Beware the Blood Moon. This update for Fallout 76 will release simultaneously on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S to improve the overall performance, stability, and visual fidelity for the game on those consoles.

After a rocky launch back in 2018, Fallout 76 has seen a massive glow-up over the years in terms of gameplay and content available to players. As the sole mainline Fallout experience of the past eight years, Fallout 76 has seen major updates that expanded its map with Skyline Valley and Burning Springs updates, the latter adding the Ghoul from the Fallout Amazon Prime show to the game. Players can even become a ghoul in Fallout 76 themselves, which is the perfect way to experience the Appalachian Wasteland in this next-gen update.

Fallout 76 Making Big Change Based On Player Feedback

Fallout 76 developer Bethesda announces a major change to the hit open-world RPG following an overwhelmingly one-sided round of player feedback.

By Dominik Bošnjak

Fallout 76's Next-Gen Update for PS5, Xbox Series X/S Arrives September 15

An official announcement from Bethesda via Twitter revealed that the upcoming Beware the Blood Moon season for Fallout 76 will also debut the next-gen update for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. The announcement regarding this update reads:

"Along with this content, our Gen 9 boost that benefits players on XBOX Series S/X, PS5, and older consoles will arrive. All console players will enjoy better performance, stability, and visual fidelity. This upgrade also affords our team the opportunity to optimize each platform individually down the road."

The Fallout 76 community manager also noted on the game's official subreddit that there are still plans for a PTS test period of this next-gen update for consoles in the coming weeks before its launch. However, no specific date was given for this test period.

It's not just the next-gen update coming on September 15 either. Fallout 76 has also announced "The Slasher," a first-of-its-kind experience that will be included in this update as a frightening new experience within the Beware the Blood Moon season. Players will uncover the mystery of Fallout 76 's Slasher over the course of a few weeks, discovering clues and battling fanatics as they hunt for this creature terrorizing the wasteland. As a reward for their efforts, Fallout 76 players who defeat The Slasher will earn a new set of unique Power Armor and the Super Slasher weapon.

Bethesda has also announced that Legacy Seasons will be returning to Fallout 76 , allowing players to earn rewards that they may have missed out on from past seasons. Each regular season of Fallout 76 will include a Legacy Season running alongside it, which will use the same pool of tickets as the normal season. The Legacy Season planned for Season 26 will be Armor Ace and the Power Patrol in Cold Steel, which first released back in September 2020.

Fallout Releases Real-Life Nuka Cola and Sunset Sarsaparilla Drinks Ahead of Season 2

'You're Going To Lose Some of Your Audience' Fallout Creator on Why Bigger RPGs Aren't Always Better

Looking ahead to 2027, Fallout 76 has confirmed that a major expansion featuring Raven Rock from Fallout 3 will be released. This expansion will act as a prequel story to Fallout 3 ahead of the Fallout 3 remaster confirmed to be in development. No specific release date has been nailed down for this expansion yet, but it sounds like Fallout 76 players will have tons of content to dive into in the meantime.

item.title: Xbox Insider Teases Surprising Announcement at Gamescom 2026
item.description:
Xbox could be hiding a surprise announcement at Gamescom 2026, according to a reliable insider. The company is reportedly planning to reveal an unexpected new entry in a series during Gamescom Opening Night Live, which airs August 25. Although it's not exactly clear what game Xbox could be announcing at this event, that hasn't stopped fans from speculating on what long-forgotten franchise might be getting a revival.

The year has already seen major shake-ups at Xbox, with new CEO Asha Sharma recommitting to Xbox exclusivity and its major IPs. Recently, the CEO shared that she got to experience The Elder Scrolls 6 while teasing the game's subtitle, sending fans into a frenzy over Bethesda's highly anticipated RPG. Other major Xbox franchises like Fallout , Fable , and Gears of War are all getting releases in the near future, and another unexpected franchise is allegedly set to join this lineup.

Brand-New Leaked Xbox Controller Spotted in the Wild

An unreleased Xbox controller somehow finds its way onto the market, revealing some potential new design, features, and buttons.

By Mohsen Baqery

Xbox Reportedly Announcing an Unexpected Sequel at Gamescom

According to a Patreon post from notable Xbox insider Jez Corden, Xbox is planning to unveil a new entry in an unexpected franchise at Gamescom. However, the details surrounding what game this could be are vague. Early fan reactions immediately jumped to long-dead Xbox-owned franchises like Rare's Banjo-Kazooie or Blizzard's StarCraft , with some hopeful fans even anticipating a re-reveal of The Elder Scrolls 6 .

Game of Thrones Fans Officially Need to Circle August 25 on Their Calendars

Game of Thrones fans need to pay attention to Tuesday, August 25 and mark their calendars accordingly.

Hogwarts Legacy 2 Officially Announced Ahead of Gamescom

Warner Bros. Discovery officially acknowledges and announces the upcoming sequel to Hogwarts Legacy.

Official New Fable Event Confirmed for August 26

Developer Playground Games and publisher Xbox officially confirm a new event showcasing Fable's gameplay for August 26.

This information was corroborated by fellow leaker NateTheHate on Twitter, who provided more context for which game franchises could be the recipient of the announcement. According to Nate, the game is not related to Banjo-Kazooie , StarCraft , or Wolfenstein , and hasn't been previously announced, ruling out The Elder Scrolls 6 or the Fallout 3 and New Vegas remasters. The game is said to be an entry in a somewhat modern, existing franchise, leading fans to suggest some pretty good potential options, such as:

  • Sequel to Ryse: Son of Rome
  • New Ori game
  • Quantum Break sequel

  • The Evil Within 3
